comments.author: zone411
comments.text: For context, OpenAI's 4 new papers resolve 8 problems of the Top 500 Open Problems in Math list (LLM ranked, https://proofatlas.ai/open-problems/ ). They include: #25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture. #89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for #64 — Mean-payoff games, #65 — Parity games, #340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games. #183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes, #130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart. #137 — Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. For every fixed number of petals r, the paper proves the conjectured Cᵣᵏ bound. (rankings post Riemann (#2) and VP vs VNP (#31)).

If they were playing this game, public model quality would stall as compute shifted to internal research, and occasional releases like this would provide a glimpse of more beneath the surface. comments.author: StableAlkyne
comments.text: We've seen so much interesting work come out of OpenAI and Anthropic in the last few weeks. It really feels like both have tapped into the pioneering spirit of the old Bell Labs. But, Bell Labs existed as part of an agreement with the government that AT&T's monopoly would be used for the public good. OpenAI and Anthropic don't really have much use for this beyond PR... If even the prestige from Riemann's Hypothesis couldn't boost ANT, what is the reason for them devoting such a huge fraction of their R&D budget to unrelated (though impactful) problems? Scaring mathematicians into burning their non-existent research budgets on tokens in order to make a couple million dollars? Open weight models are to the point that most business cases are completely solved by them, at a fraction of the price of Claude, Copilot, or OpenAI. Unfortunately, the average business doesn't care that the AI can solve frontier problems: they just need something to summarize emails or give an executive a summary of the day's headlines. The market is just waiting for a cheap provider that is just as turnkey... Which isn't exactly a high barrier these days. IMO there is space for a unicorn to emerge in the next few years to eat everyone's lunch.

comments.author: amluto
comments.text: This shared LV cache thing is, in my mind, ridiculous. Web browser developers learned, quite a while ago, that caches need to be separated for different origins. Inference servers should add a similar feature: allow API calls to specify cache separation keys that prevent one security context from probing another context’s cache. As for the step size issue, Google recently had a post about producing exactly consistent output across different kernels (specifically by defining a deterministic prefill algorithm and then requiring all kernels to generate results exactly equal to prefilling on the sequence in question). More broadly, I think it’s a bit odd to frame this as “models” communicating. This is software communicating, and the models happen to be running the software.

comments.author: devy
comments.text: Frontier models today can easily figure this out. The less frontier models as of right now are probably going to take a long horizon session to figure out this type of "side channel" comms. comments.author: kgeist
comments.text: If a single vLLM instance handles both prefill and decode without disaggregation, I can think of another way. Alice reads a long document every N seconds to transmit a 1, and does nothing to transmit a 0. Bob, in its own loop, measures the time using bash, generates some random text and writes it to a file, and then checks the time again to estimate its own tokens per second (file length / elapsed time). The trick is that when a vLLM instance handles both prefill and decode, decoding slows down measurably because vLLM has to alternate between prefill and decode phases. It assumes only 2 agents are running, though, but it doesn't require fine-tuning or a second helper model.

comments.author: gopalv
comments.text: > We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models. The ability to write code is basically the superpower for these models. Even math, the models were worse off before Lean was accepted as output.

comments.author: fabian2k
comments.text: > To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target. I don't get it. What did GTP-6.2 actually design here? The sequence is the structure for proteins. So did the model output a sequence here as answer to a question like "design a protein for target X" or not? To me, "protein design" means you have a goal and you create a sequence that achieves that goal. I'm also not sure what a "three-dimensional design" would be in this case. Charges matter a lot for binding, as do hydrophobic areas. At sufficient resolution you're again at an amino acid sequence in a specific fold with that. Or did GPT-6.2 just design a rough tertiary structure here (helices, beta sheets and loops) and the details were filled in by the specialized model?

comments.author: plaidfuji
comments.text: This is interesting, although the “beyond specialized models” feels a bit premature. It seems like GPT can act like a glue layer between the highly specialized models that carry out each specific sub-task in a protein design workflow… and in some cases, can outperform specialized models at those tasks. I’ve noticed that LLMs are very good at this type of glue work between highly specialized fields. It used to be quite difficult to “connect” your own work to adjacent tools made by other SMEs, sometimes so difficult that it was impractical. I suspect one of the biggest impacts of LLMs on science will be the enablement of more frictionless collaboration and higher-level integration of specialized capabilities in a single study. That said, the use of “intrinsic design capabilities” in the title of this article is misleading, as much of the demonstrated capabilities involve tool calls, and/or need outside support by the same specialized models they claim to have moved beyond in order to arrive at useful results.

comments.author: Xcelerate
comments.text: I heard an interesting question once: if we consider all the greatest discoveries of mankind and imagine a counterfactual world where their discoverer had not existed, how many additional years would it have taken for someone else to have made the discovery? Subjectively, I think most of the major discoveries would have only been delayed by a decade or two. E.g., general relativity, quantum mechanics, the laws of thermodynamics. For the incompleteness theorems, however, I’m not sure that we would even be aware of them today without Gödel. Tarski might have come the closest, but there were still a few insane conceptual leaps that had to be made beyond the undefinability of truth. The theorems are often considered a curiosity at the edges of mathematics, but I’m not so sure. I think they might be more fundamental than typically given credit for. The problem is that the theorems aren’t really actionable since they rule out essentially all algorithmic methods of working around the limitations they entail.

comments.author: asdff
comments.text: It takes some learning curve, but a skateboard is actually a really good way to get around an urban area. Biggest pluses are you can tuck it away anywhere, but unlike a folding bike, you can use it instantly. You end up saving time in all sorts of places that would be inappropriate with other vehicles, thanks to the speed differential being closer to a couple mile an hour walking than most other micro mobility that's closer to a 25mph car. Biking down the mezzanine to the train platform is a little egregious, but pushing a skateboard out of anyone's way is perfectly reasonable, and might save you quite a lot of time to make that train connection. Any clear patch of 25 feet in front of you, you might as well skate it in a half second.
